verses.translation: Now, therefore, the inquiry into bhakti.
verses.commentary: Shandilya opens with almost the same formula as Narada — "athāto" — and almost the same as the Brahma Sutras ("athāto brahma-jijñāsā"). The parallel is deliberate: Shandilya places the inquiry into bhakti at the same philosophical level as the inquiry into Brahman. Just as the Brahma Sutras ask "what is Brahman?" Shandilya asks "what is bhakti?" — treating it not as a subordinate practice but as an independent object of philosophical investigation deserving its own systematic treatment. The word "jijñāsā" (inquiry, the desire to know) frames this as an intellectual and spiritual quest together: you cannot understand bhakti from outside; you must become a bhakta-jijñāsu — one who both practises and seeks to understand.

verses.science: अब अतः भक्ति की जिज्ञासा। श्रद्धा और सुरक्षित लगाव तनाव-प्रतिक्रिया को घटाते हैं। यह पंक्ति उसी आश्रय को अपना विषय बनाती है।

verses.translation: That (bhakti) is supreme attachment (para-anurakti) to Ishvara.
verses.hindi: वह (भक्ति) ईश्वर में परानुरक्ति (परम आसक्ति) है।
verses.commentary: Shandilya's definition in four words. "Para-anurakti" — supreme attachment. "Anurakti" differs from "prema" (Narada's term): anurakti carries the connotation of sustained, deepening attachment that grows over time — the kind of love that binds a devoted disciple to a teacher, a child to a parent, a true devotee to their chosen form of the divine. "Para" (supreme) distinguishes this from ordinary worldly attachment (which Shandilya will discuss as an obstacle to bhakti). And the direction: "Ishvare" — in or toward Ishvara. Not a diffuse spirituality but a specific, directed attachment to the divine reality. The comparison with Narada: Narada says bhakti IS love; Shandilya says bhakti is ATTACHMENT — the ongoing quality of being drawn toward and held by the divine.

verses.translation: Ishvara is the supreme Lord — omniscient, omnipotent, the inner controller of all.
verses.hindi: ईश्वर परमेश्वर है — सर्वज्ञ, सर्वशक्तिमान, और सबका अन्तर्यामी।
verses.commentary: Shandilya immediately follows his definition of bhakti with a definition of its object: Ishvara. Three attributes — sarvajña (all-knowing), sarvaśaktimān (all-powerful), sarvāntaryāmī (inner controller of all). The third is the most philosophically significant: "antaryāmī" — the one who dwells within all, who is the innermost witness and controller of every being. This is not a distant God to whom petitions are sent; it is the divine that is more intimate to you than your own thoughts, the one who knows you more completely than you know yourself. Bhakti directed at this Ishvara is not an outward gesture but an inner recognition.

verses.translation: That alone (is both means and end), because there is no difference between the goal and the means.
verses.hindi: वही (भक्ति) साध्य और साधन दोनों है — क्योंकि साध्य और साधन में कोई भेद नहीं है।
verses.commentary: One of Shandilya's most philosophically precise sutras: bhakti is both the sādhana (means/practice) and the sādhya (goal/end). This collapses the structure of most spiritual frameworks in which practice is instrumental — a means to a separate end. In bhakti, the means and the end are the same substance: love. You do not practise love to arrive at love. The practice of love IS the presence of love. The moment genuine bhakti arises, the goal is already present. This is why Narada says bhakti is self-proving: it requires no external fruit to validate itself because the practice and its highest expression are identical.

verses.sanskrit: न तु तद्विना ज्ञानं भक्तेः साधनत्वेन | तस्य फलत्वात् ||
verses.transliteration: na tu tadvina jñānaṃ bhakteḥ sādhanaTvena | tasya phalatvāt ||
verses.translation: But knowledge is not the means (sadhana) to bhakti without that (Ishvara). Because (bhakti) is its fruit.
verses.hindi: परन्तु ईश्वर के बिना ज्ञान भक्ति का साधन नहीं है। क्योंकि (भक्ति) उसका फल है।
verses.commentary: Shandilya's most subtle sutra: knowledge (jnana) is not the means (sadhana) to bhakti — bhakti is the fruit of knowledge rightly understood. This inverts the common assumption that you first gain jnana and then, as a result, develop bhakti. Shandilya says: when jnana is genuine — when the knowledge of Ishvara's nature is real and not merely intellectual — bhakti arises spontaneously as its fruit. You do not produce bhakti by trying to love; you produce it by truly knowing the one you are loving. The more deeply you know Ishvara, the more naturally love arises. Knowledge and love are not two stages; they are two aspects of the same deepening.

verses.translation: Actions done for His sake are also limbs of bhakti.
verses.hindi: उसके लिए किये गये कर्म भी भक्ति के अंग हैं।
verses.commentary: Shandilya integrates karma into bhakti with surgical precision: actions performed "for His sake" (tadArthe — for the sake of Ishvara) are not separate from bhakti but are its limbs (aṅgas). This resolves the apparent tension between the path of action (karma-yoga) and the path of devotion (bhakti-yoga): they are not different paths but one path with two aspects. Any action whatsoever — cooking, working, raising children, serving the sick — when offered to Ishvara as the ultimate beneficiary and witness, becomes a limb of bhakti. The Bhagavad Gita's teaching on karma-yoga (act without attachment, offer the fruits to the divine) is here integrated into the bhakti framework.

verses.translation: From the fault of wrong company, from attachment to unworthy sense-objects — and from the opposite of these (right company and detachment) comes bhakti.
verses.hindi: कुसंग के दोष से और अयोग्य विषयों में राग से (भक्ति में विघ्न होता है) — और इनके विपरीत से (भक्ति होती है)।
verses.commentary: Shandilya identifies the two primary obstacles to bhakti — and their remedy — with characteristic economy. "Saṅga-doṣa" (the fault of wrong company): the single most reliable predictor of a person's spiritual development is the company they keep. Those who are around people who mock devotion, who treat the sacred casually, who live entirely for sensory gratification — their bhakti slowly suffocates. "Asat-viṣaya-rāga" (attachment to unworthy objects): the attention that should flow toward Ishvara is captured by objects that cannot satisfy. The remedy is simply stated as "tad-vipārīta" — the opposite: right company (satsang) and detachment from objects that dissipate attention.

verses.translation: The offering of all actions to Ishvara — and through His remembrance alone.
verses.hindi: सभी कर्मों को ईश्वर में अर्पण करना — और केवल उसके स्मरण से।
verses.commentary: The Shandilya Bhakti Sutras' practical summary: two instruments for removing obstacles and deepening bhakti — arpaṇa (offering all actions) and smṛti (remembrance). These correspond directly to the Bhagavad Gita's karma-yoga and jnana-yoga integrated into bhakti: offer every action (karma-arpaṇa) and maintain continuous remembrance (smaranam). Together these two practices transform the entire field of experience — action and cognition — into a continuous stream of devotion. Nothing is excluded: not work, not rest, not mundane tasks. Everything becomes an offering; everything becomes a remembrance.

verses.translation: For the devotee, all undertakings succeed of themselves.
verses.hindi: भक्त के सभी कार्य स्वयमेव सिद्ध होते हैं।
verses.commentary: The most practically reassuring sutra of the Shandilya Bhakti Sutras. "Svataḥ sidhyanti" — succeed of themselves, spontaneously, without laboured effort. This is not a promise that the bhakta will get whatever they want; it is a description of how the bhakta's actions become effortless and effective when they flow from a centre of genuine devotion. Actions aligned with one's deepest nature and offered to Ishvara do not require the same anxious effort as actions driven by ego and fear. They arise from a different source and produce different quality results — not always what the ego wanted, but always what is genuinely needed.

verses.science: सभी कर्मों को ईश्वर में अर्पण करना — और केवल उसके स्मरण से। जो बार-बार किया जाता है, वह अगली प्रवृत्ति को मजबूत करता है। यह पंक्ति कर्म को उसी चक्र के रूप में देखती है।

chapters.title: The Fruits of Bhakti — What Devotion Produces

verses.translation: Through that (bhakti), liberation as union with the Blessed Lord.
verses.hindi: उस (भक्ति) से भगवान के साथ सायुज्य-मुक्ति होती है।
verses.commentary: Shandilya specifies the form of liberation that bhakti produces: "sāyujya-mukti" — liberation as union. In the classical classification of four types of mukti (sālokya — dwelling in the same world, sārūpya — having the same form, sāmīpya — being near, and sāyujya — being one with), sāyujya is the highest. The bhakta does not want proximity to the divine; they want union. Not to visit, not to resemble, not to dwell nearby — but to merge. And yet this union does not destroy the devotee: Shandilya's framework preserves the distinction of the lover and the beloved even in the highest state, because love requires two. This is the great debate between Advaita (non-dual) and Dvaita (dual) — and Shandilya quietly sides with the bhakti position: the sweetness of union depends on the persistence of the lover.

verses.translation: For the devotee, all undertakings succeed of themselves.
verses.hindi: भक्त के सभी कार्य स्वयमेव सिद्ध होते हैं।
verses.commentary: The most practically reassuring sutra of the Shandilya Bhakti Sutras. "Svataḥ sidhyanti" — succeed of themselves, spontaneously, without laboured effort. This is not a promise that the bhakta will get whatever they want; it is a description of how the bhakta's actions become effortless and effective when they flow from a centre of genuine devotion. Actions aligned with one's deepest nature and offered to Ishvara do not require the same anxious effort as actions driven by ego and fear. They arise from a different source and produce different quality results — not always what the ego wanted, but always what is genuinely needed.
